name: Zuranolone (Zurzuvae)
summary: 14-day, once-nightly oral treatment for postpartum depression that can start working within days. Strong sedation + driving impairment risk, and it must be taken with a fat-containing meal.
description: Zurzuvae (zuranolone) is a short-course postpartum depression medication you take once nightly for 14 days. Many people notice mood symptoms improve quickly (sometimes within a few days). The tradeoff: it can make you very sleepy, foggy, and unsafe to drive—so you need a full 12-hour no-driving window after each dose. It also has abuse and physical-dependence potential, even though the treatment course is brief. Always take it with a fat-containing meal so it actually absorbs.
patient_summary: Zurzuvae is a 14-day, once-nightly pill for postpartum depression that may start helping within days. Biggest risks are heavy sleepiness, confusion, and driving impairment—no driving for 12 hours after each dose. Take it with a fat-containing meal. It’s a controlled substance and can cause dependence/withdrawal symptoms if used longer or at higher doses than prescribed.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Antidepressant; Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid (GABA) A Receptor Positive Modulator

linked_conditions.context: FDA-approved for postpartum depression in adults as a short, 14-day nightly course. It’s designed for faster symptom relief than traditional antidepressants, with sedation and driving impairment as the big limiting factors.
Not FDA-approved for major depressive disorder. If you’re being treated for non-postpartum depression, this usually isn’t the medication your clinician reaches for first.

contraindications: No contraindications listed in manufacturer labeling

efficacy_response.comparison_data: Least-squares mean change -15.6 with zuranolone vs -11.6 with placebo (difference -4.0) in a Phase 3 trial using 50 mg/day for 14 days.
efficacy_response.patient_text: In a large clinical trial for severe postpartum depression, people taking zuranolone improved more than placebo by Day 15 on a standard depression scale—and the separation showed up as early as Day 3 in the study.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Food-dependent; must be taken with a fat-containing meal for adequate absorption
pharmacokinetics.onset: Clinical improvement reported as early as Day 3 in trials; sedating effects can occur after dosing
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily hepatic via CYP3A4; no active metabolites
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Fat-containing meals markedly increase exposure; high-fat meals increase Cmax ~4.3-fold and AUC ~2-fold; smaller fat-containing meals increase Cmax ~3.5-fold and AUC ~1.8-fold

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Zurzuvae (zuranolone) is FDA-approved to treat {link:condition:postpartum-depression:postpartum depression} in adults. It’s a short, fixed course (14 nights) and it’s built for faster symptom relief than the typical “wait weeks” antidepressant story.
items: {link:condition:postpartum-depression:Postpartum Depression (PPD)}: Depression that starts after childbirth (and can seriously affect mood, sleep, functioning, and bonding)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Zurzuvae has a very “body-forward” feel for a depression medication: some people notice mood lift quickly, but sedation can be intense. Here’s what tends to come up:

quotes: I didn’t feel “fixed,” but I felt less trapped pretty quickly.
By a few days in, the heaviness started easing up.
It was the first time postpartum that my brain felt like it had oxygen again.
items.note: In clinical trials, improvement on depression ratings separated from placebo as early as Day 3.

items.category: Sleepiness, sedation, and the “I’m not driving” reality
quotes: It knocked me out. Like—plan your night around it.
I felt calmer but also kind of drunk-tired.
My body was sleepy even when my mind wanted to do things.
items.note: Driving impairment is a core safety issue. You need a full 12-hour no-driving window after each dose during the 14-day course.

quotes: I was more forgetful than usual—like postpartum brain turned up.
My thoughts felt slowed down, not in a peaceful way—just… slower.
I had moments of confusion that freaked me out.
items.note: Memory impairment and confusion are reported. If you feel confused or unsafe, call your prescriber.

quotes: I felt dizzy, especially when I stood up fast.
It was like mild vertigo some nights.
I had to move slower because I felt wobbly.
items.note: Falls are a real risk because of sedation + dizziness—especially if you’re already sleep-deprived postpartum.

items.category: Anxiety can still show up (sometimes oddly)
quotes: My depression improved but my anxiety still popped in.
I felt tired but weirdly restless at times.
I had a couple nights of jittery anxiety.
items.note: Anxiety has been reported as a side effect. If anxiety spikes hard, tell your clinician promptly.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: This is a short-course medication: you take it nightly for 14 days. Mood benefits can start within days, but sedation can also hit hard after dosing.
key_points: Nightly dosing: Taken once per evening for 14 days
Day 3: Clinical trials showed separation from placebo on depression scores as early as Day 3
Day 15: Primary outcome timepoint in Phase 3 trials (end of the 14-day dosing window)
5-6 hours: Time to peak blood levels after dosing
~20-25 hours: Approximate half-life (it doesn’t vanish overnight)
Food matters: Must be taken with a fat-containing meal or absorption drops a lot

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: In a Phase 3 postpartum depression trial, zuranolone improved depression scores more than placebo by Day 15, with differences showing up as early as Day 3 and persisting beyond the dosing window in the study follow-up.
sections.clinical_details: In a double-blind Phase 3 trial in severe postpartum depression (N=196), participants received zuranolone 50 mg daily or placebo for 14 days. The primary endpoint was change in HAM-D (17-item) total score at Day 15. The least-squares mean change was -15.6 with zuranolone vs -11.6 with placebo (difference -4.0; 95% CI -6.3 to -1.7).

citation.title: Zuranolone for the Treatment of Postpartum Depression

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: No driving (or other hazardous activities) for at least 12 hours after every dose during the 14-day course.
sections.black_box: WARNING: IMPAIRED ABILITY TO DRIVE OR ENGAGE IN OTHER POTENTIALLY HAZARDOUS ACTIVITIES. Zuranolone causes driving impairment due to central nervous system (CNS) depressant effects. Patients should not drive or engage in potentially hazardous activities until at least 12 hours after administration for the duration of the 14-day treatment course. Patients may not be able to assess their own driving competence or the degree of impairment.
other: CNS depression: Can cause marked drowsiness, sedation, and confusion—your brain may be slower than you realize
Falls: Sedation + dizziness + postpartum sleep deprivation is a bad mix. Move slowly and get support if you feel unsteady
Suicidal thinking/behavior: Antidepressants can increase suicidality risk in some people (especially ages 18-24). Monitor closely during treatment and for 1-2 months after
Abuse and misuse: This is a Schedule IV controlled substance with abuse potential
Physical dependence and withdrawal symptoms: Withdrawal-type symptoms have been reported after stopping, especially with higher-than-recommended doses or longer-than-recommended use
patient_counseling: Plan a 12-hour no-driving window after every dose. If you take it at 9pm, don’t drive until at least 9am the next day.
Assume you’re more impaired than you feel. People often cannot accurately judge their own level of impairment on this medication.
Avoid alcohol and be extremely cautious with other sedating meds (sleep meds, benzos, opioids, antihistamines).
Tell your prescriber immediately if depression worsens, you feel agitated or unusually irritable, or you have any suicidal thoughts.
Do not extend the course or “keep it going” without medical guidance. The regimen is intentionally short.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: sleepiness/sedation and dizziness. Some people also feel foggy, forgetful, or confused. Because you’re postpartum (sleep-deprived, physically recovering), these effects can hit harder than you expect.

common.patient_note: This is the big one. If you’re trying to function at night (feeding, pumping, checking on baby), plan support. Take it only when you can commit to being slowed down.
Stand up slowly, especially at night. If you feel wobbly, don’t carry the baby while walking around the house.
Hydrate and watch for dehydration, especially if you’re breastfeeding or already not eating well postpartum.
Postpartum fatigue is already intense. This can stack on top of it and make you feel flattened.
If you have burning, urgency, or fever, don’t ignore it—postpartum UTIs can escalate quickly.
If you notice forgetfulness, write things down and avoid decisions that need sharp judgment at night.
Can overlap with postpartum recovery. If pain is severe or persistent, rule out other causes.
Yes, ironically. If anxiety ramps up, or you feel agitated/restless, report it.
Usually mild, but if it’s intense or scary, check in with your clinician.
If rash spreads rapidly, blisters, or you have swelling/trouble breathing, seek urgent care.

serious: Confusion: frequency not defined; can be dangerous, especially overnight when caring for an infant
Severe sedation or altered consciousness: overdose risk exists; seek emergency care if someone is difficult to wake or not acting normal
Worsening depression or emergent suicidality: requires urgent clinical evaluation
Falls and injuries: sedation + dizziness increases risk; this is especially relevant postpartum

Withdrawal-type symptoms after stopping (reported in healthy subjects after several days of dosing): insomnia, palpitations, decreased appetite, nightmares, nausea, sweating, paranoia—risk may be higher if used longer or at higher doses than recommended

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Zurzuvae is a CYP3A4 substrate and it’s also a CNS depressant. So two big interaction buckets matter: (1) meds that change CYP3A4 levels and (2) anything else that sedates you.

items.risk: Can raise zuranolone levels and increase sedation, confusion, and impairment.
items.action: Expect dose adjustments or avoidance depending on the interacting drug. Your prescriber should explicitly review this before starting.

items.with: CYP3A4 inducers (including some seizure meds and herbal products)
items.risk: Can lower zuranolone levels and reduce benefit (and make the course feel like it “did nothing”).
items.action: Avoid when possible or choose alternatives. Tell your clinician about all supplements—especially St. John’s Wort.

items.risk: Additive CNS depression: worse sedation, worse impairment, higher fall risk, and potentially dangerous oversedation.
items.action: Avoid alcohol during the 14-day course (and be cautious for at least several days after if you still feel sedated).

items.with: Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sleep meds, sedating antihistamines, muscle relaxants, cannabis/THC)
items.risk: Stacking sedation can push you into unsafe territory (confusion, falls, impaired caregiving, dangerous driving impairment).
items.action: Avoid combining when possible. If something sedating is medically necessary, your prescriber should plan it intentionally and monitor closely.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: For the FDA-approved use, Zurzuvae is a short, 14-day course—so most people finish the course and stop without a formal taper. The big rule is: do not extend the treatment or increase dose on your own. Withdrawal-type symptoms have been reported after stopping, and the risk appears higher with higher-than-recommended doses or longer-than-recommended use.
key_points: Standard course: 14 days total (nightly). Most patients do not need a taper after completing the labeled regimen.
Do not self-extend: Using longer than recommended or at higher doses may increase dependence and withdrawal risk.
Possible withdrawal-type symptoms (reported after stopping in healthy subjects): insomnia, palpitations, decreased appetite, nightmares, nausea, sweating, paranoia.
If you feel withdrawal symptoms: contact your prescriber—do not restart or adjust dosing on your own.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Zurzuvae is taken once nightly for 14 days, in the evening, with a fat-containing meal. The dosing is intentionally simple—and the safety rules (food + no driving window) are non-negotiable.

adult.ppd_standard: 50 mg PO once daily in the evening for 14 days
adult.ppd_tolerability_reduction: If CNS depressant effects are a problem (too sleepy, too foggy), reduce to 40 mg PO once daily in the evening for 14 days
adult.with_food: Take with a fat-containing meal (400 to 1,000 calories; 25% to 50% fat) for adequate absorption
adult.missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take the next dose at the regularly scheduled time the next evening. Do not take an extra dose the same day.
adult.renal: eGFR ≥60: no adjustment. eGFR 15 to 59: 30 mg PO once daily in the evening for 14 days. eGFR <15 or dialysis: not studied (no labeled adjustment guidance).
adult.hepatic: Child-Turcotte-Pugh A or B: no adjustment. Child-Turcotte-Pugh C: 30 mg PO once daily in the evening for 14 days.
adult.elderly: Refer to adult dosing; not specifically studied in older adults.

sections.simple_explanation: This is a fixed, 14-night course. You take it in the evening because it commonly makes people sleepy. The meal requirement matters because fat dramatically increases absorption—without it, the medication exposure can be much lower.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Zurzuvae is used after delivery for postpartum depression, but pregnancy and breastfeeding still matter. If you could become pregnant, contraception planning matters. If you’re breastfeeding, the decision is shared and practical (timing, pumping, and your goals).
sections.pregnancy: Based on animal reproduction data, in utero exposure may cause fetal harm. Because postpartum depression can begin late in pregnancy, treatment decisions during pregnancy typically favor other options if antidepressant treatment must start before delivery. Shared decision-making is essential.
sections.lactation: Zuranolone is present in breast milk. Available data suggest very low infant exposure (relative infant dose <1% in a small study of lactating women given 30 mg daily for 5 days), and milk concentrations fell below quantification several days after the last dose. The manufacturer recommends weighing infant exposure risk, breastfeeding benefits, and treatment benefits. Until more data exist, an option is pumping and discarding milk during therapy and for 1 week after the last dose.
sections.geriatrics: Not specifically studied. Use adult dosing, but be extra cautious about sedation, confusion, and falls.
sections.hepatic: Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Turcotte-Pugh C): 30 mg nightly for 14 days; increased exposure is expected. Use caution and monitor sedation/impairment.
sections.renal: Moderate to severe renal impairment (eGFR 15 to 59): 30 mg nightly for 14 days; exposure increases when eGFR <60. Not studied in eGFR <15 or dialysis.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Sedation and impairment: drowsiness, slowed thinking, confusion—especially during the first few nights and after any dose reduction decisions
Driving and safety behaviors: confirm the patient is reliably keeping the 12-hour no-driving/no-hazard window after each dose
Falls risk: dizziness/vertigo, unsteadiness, nighttime caregiving, sleep deprivation, and any other sedating medications
Suicidality and clinical worsening: monitor closely during treatment and for 1-2 months after (especially ages 18-24), and involve family/caregivers when appropriate
Behavioral activation signals: agitation, irritability, insomnia, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania/mania-like symptoms—report immediately
Misuse/abuse risk: early refill requests, taking more than prescribed, using for a “high,” combining with alcohol/other sedatives
Dependence/withdrawal-type symptoms: insomnia, palpitations, sweating, nightmares, nausea, paranoia after stopping—especially if the course is extended or dosing is higher than recommended
Medication interaction review: CYP3A4 inhibitor/inducer checks at start (and again if meds change mid-course)

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Zurzuvae is an oral capsule taken once nightly with a fat-containing meal.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Zurzuvae is a positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors. In plain terms: it boosts the brain’s main calming system. The exact reason this helps postpartum depression isn’t fully mapped out, but the working idea is that stabilizing GABA-A signaling can rapidly reduce depressive symptoms in the postpartum period.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Zurzuvae fills a very specific lane: postpartum depression that needs faster symptom relief than traditional antidepressants, with a short, time-limited dosing plan. It’s not a casual medication—you have to plan around sedation and the 12-hour driving restriction—but for the right patient, the speed can be meaningful. It can be used as a standalone rapid intervention or alongside longer-term supports like therapy and/or maintenance antidepressants, depending on severity, relapse risk, and patient preference.

seo.title: Zuranolone (Zurzuvae): Postpartum Depression Uses, Dosing, Side Effects & Safety
seo.description: Zurzuvae (zuranolone) is a 14-day, once-nightly oral treatment for postpartum depression. Learn dosing (50 mg nightly), why you must take it with a fat-containing meal, common side effects (sleepiness, dizziness), the 12-hour no-driving rule, interactions, and dependence risk.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Zurzuvae (zuranolone) is FDA-approved for postpartum depression in adults. It’s taken once nightly for 14 days and is designed for faster symptom relief than many traditional antidepressants.

In clinical trials, improvement on depression scores separated from placebo as early as Day 3, with the main outcome measured at Day 15 (right after the 14-night course). Some people feel change within days, but everyone’s timeline is different.

faqs.q: Why do I have to take Zurzuvae with a fat-containing meal?
faqs.a: Because absorption depends heavily on food—fat increases drug exposure a lot. If you take it without a fat-containing meal, you may absorb much less medication and get less benefit. The standard guidance is a meal around 400 to 1,000 calories with 25% to 50% fat.

faqs.q: Can I drive after taking Zurzuvae?
faqs.a: No—do not drive or do other dangerous activities until at least 12 hours after each dose during the entire 14-day course. This medication can impair driving, and people often cannot accurately judge how impaired they are.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: The most common side effects are drowsiness/somnolence and dizziness (including vertigo). People can also feel fatigued, foggy, forgetful, or occasionally confused. Because postpartum life already includes sleep deprivation, the sedation can feel extra intense.
Yes. Zurzuvae is Schedule IV. It has abuse potential, and physical dependence/withdrawal-type symptoms have been reported—especially with higher-than-recommended doses or longer-than-recommended use.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off Zurzuvae?
faqs.a: Usually not for the FDA-approved regimen, because it’s a short 14-day course. The bigger rule is: don’t extend the course or increase dose on your own. If you have withdrawal-type symptoms after stopping, contact your prescriber.

faqs.q: What if I miss a dose?
faqs.a: Skip it and take your next dose at the regular time the next evening. Do not take an extra dose on the same day to make up for a missed dose.

faqs.q: Can I take Zurzuvae if I have kidney or liver problems?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but dosing changes may be needed. With eGFR 15 to 59, the recommended dose is 30 mg nightly for 14 days. With severe liver impairment (Child-Turcotte-Pugh C), the recommended dose is also 30 mg nightly for 14 days. It hasn’t been studied in eGFR <15 or dialysis.

faqs.q: Can I breastfeed while taking Zurzuvae?
faqs.a: Zuranolone is present in breast milk, and limited data suggest low infant exposure, but guidance is still evolving. The manufacturer recommends shared decision-making that weighs infant exposure risk, breastfeeding benefits, and treatment benefits. An option some clinicians discuss is pumping and discarding milk during therapy and for 1 week after the last dose.

faqs.q: Does Zurzuvae replace therapy or standard antidepressants?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. It’s a short-course, rapid option for postpartum depression, and it may be used alongside therapy and/or longer-term medications depending on symptom severity, relapse risk, and what you and your clinician decide together.
